conformance-concrete.doc:
Concrete-input conformance claims.

Each claim runs a FULLY CONCRETE program through `#run` and asserts the exact final `<pc>` and
`<status>`. A concrete claim that proves under kprove is the operational equivalent of having
`krun` the program: it establishes "this exact input reaches this exact state" under the K
rules. (krun proper hangs on revert-producing cases in this environment for both the stock
`swapvm-llvm` build and any build importing the opcode modules; concrete kprove claims bypass
that tooling bug and use the working Haskell backend.)

The hand-derived expectations here are cross-checked against the Solidity side in
`test/conformance/InstructionConformance.t.sol` (`test_conformance_<opcode>_concrete`), which
runs the SAME bytes through the REAL instruction bodies and REAL `runLoop`. Agreement between
the two sides IS the conformance evidence -- neither side alone suffices.

Arg payloads are built with `Int2Bytes(N, V, BE)` so the byte widths are exact by construction
(hand-typing multi-byte literals miscounted on the first attempt -- a JumpIfTokenIn claim
declared argsLen 22 but supplied a 23-byte body, tripping RunLoopExceedProgramLength instead of
the rule under test).

Scope: only the direct-form opcodes whose rules reduce without uninterpreted symbols
(Salt, Revert, Jump, JumpIfDirection, JumpIfTokenIn, JumpIfTokenOut, PrivateOrder).
The opcodes whose conditions are uninterpreted predicates/functions (Deadline, Gte,
SupplyShare, TxOrigin, both Whitelists) cannot be concretely executed by kprove either -- a
concrete claim would still need a premise to fix the uninterpreted value, so it would no
longer be "fully concrete". Those are conformance-untestable in the current modelling; see the
final report. Stop is also deferred: its K rule leaves pc at the post-decode value while
Solidity sets nextPC = type(uint256).max, a documented fidelity gap that a conformance case on
the pc field would surface as a mismatch -- fixing it is a separate modelling decision.

control-sensitivity.doc:
MUST PROVE. The twin of negative-control.k: identical premises, only the conclusion
differs -- Running instead of Reverted.

This is what makes the negative control meaningful. A control that FAILS tells you
nothing unless the same setup with the RIGHT conclusion SUCCEEDS; otherwise the failure
may be incidental -- a syntax error, a missing lemma, a stuck configuration. Together the
pair shows kprove is discriminating on the conclusion and not merely choking on the setup.

deadline-concrete.doc:
Concrete-input conformance claims for the 0x20 (Deadline) opcode.

This file replaces the former `deadline-spec.k` (a symbolic universal claim) and
`deadline-control.k` (its sensitivity twin). Both were TAUTOLOGICAL under the prior
predicate-form rule: the spec assumed `#deadlineExceeded(DL)` as a premise and the rule
branched on the same predicate, so the proof established nothing about whether the underlying
`>` / `<=` matched Solidity, and krun could not reduce the predicate either — i.e. zero
conformance evidence. See deadline.md "Direct form, concrete conformance" for the full
rationale of the switch.

The direct two-arm rule in `opcodes/deadline.k` branches on the REAL comparison
#blockTimestamp() >Int DL     (REVERT)
#blockTimestamp() <=Int DL    (PASS)
mirroring the Solidity `block.timestamp > deadline` / `<= deadline` split exactly. A symbolic
universal claim over arbitrary DL does NOT prove in this form (the K Haskell backend does not
propagate an inequality premise on an uninterpreted-vs-symbolic comparison into a refutation
of the opposite arm — opcodes/deadline.md:125-156). CONCRETE claims, however, are unaffected:
with `#blockTimestamp()` fixed by a premise and DL a concrete Int, the SMT solver decides
`>Int` / `<=Int` directly and arm selection is immediate. So the two scenarios here ARE the
conformance evidence — they verify the actual comparison against Solidity for fixed inputs,
which the predicate-form symbolic proof could never do.

Each claim runs a FULLY CONCRETE program through `#run` and asserts the exact final `<pc>` and
`<status>`. A concrete claim that proves under kprove is the operational equivalent of having
`krun` the program: it establishes "this exact input reaches this exact state" under the K
rules. The hand-derived expectations here are cross-checked against the Solidity side in
`test/conformance/InstructionConformance.t.sol` (`test_conformance_deadline_*`), which runs
the SAME bytes through the REAL `_deadline` body and REAL `runLoop` — using `vm.warp(timestamp)`
to set `block.timestamp` for the run. Agreement between the two sides IS the conformance
evidence — neither side alone suffices.

PROGRAM CONSTRUCTION. Program = b"\x20\x05" +Bytes Int2Bytes(5, DL, BE) (7 bytes total).
`b"\x20\x05"` is the [opcode:1][argsLen:1] header — opcode 0x20 = 32 decimal, argsLen 0x05 = 5
decimal (the uint40 deadline). After the decode loop fires <pc> = 2 + 5 = 7. NOTE on the
opcode byte: it is `\x20` (= 32 decimal), NOT `\x14` (= 20 decimal) — the rule keys on the
DECIMAL opcode `#exec ( 32 , ARGS )` and the program byte is the hex literal 0x20 = 32. The
arg payload is built via `Int2Bytes(5, DL, BE)` so the byte width is exact by construction.

extruction-control.doc:
DELIBERATELY FALSE. Must fail.

Identical program to extruction-spec.k — Extruction (opcode 0x04, argsLen 0x14,
20-byte target TGT in [0, 2^160)) followed by a symbolic TAIL — but the conclusion
is Running instead of Reverted("ExtructionUnmodelled"). The K rule
(opcodes/extruction.k) reverts unconditionally on canonical args (length >= 20) because
the external call is an unmodelled abstraction boundary (PLAN.md D4). So this claim
cannot close, and kprove must report not-proved with a counterexample ending in
<status> Reverted("ExtructionUnmodelled") at <pc> 22.

WHY THIS SHAPE. Mirrors negative-control.k, stop-control.k, revert-control.k,
salt-control.k, and jump-control.k: the program prefix is concrete (so the prover can
actually decode opcode 0x04), the rule fires for real, and the failure is on the
conclusion — not on a stuck decode. If this control ever PROVES, the rule set is
inconsistent (e.g. the Extruction rule lost its `=> #revert(...)` rewrite) and
extruction-spec.k above is void (proofs/README.md:20-28).

The sensitivity twin is extruction-spec.k itself: same premises, correct conclusion,
must prove. Together they show kprove is discriminating on the conclusion rather than
choking on the setup.

ENV CAVEAT. Like jump-control.k and salt-control.k, this control's non-zero exit is the
meaningful signal only when kprove is healthy on the sibling positive claim. In this
sandbox kprove has been observed to die with "Haskell Backend execution failed" when
TMPDIR is not /tmp; the task brief's "Critical environment facts" #2 directs setting
TMPDIR=/tmp, which the run harness does. Under that fix the control's failure here is a
real counterexample, not incidental.

extruction-spec.doc:
T-extruction — Extruction reverts in the model with "ExtructionUnmodelled".

The real VM's _extruction (Extruction.sol:90-115) delegates to a maker-chosen external
contract whose return values overwrite <pc>, the chop cursor, and the entire <swap>
cell. That external call is an abstraction boundary (PLAN.md D4) and cannot be modelled
soundly without modelling arbitrary code. The K rule (opcodes/extruction.k) therefore
reverts loudly with "ExtructionUnmodelled" for canonical-or-longer args (>= 20 bytes),
following the same loud-not-silent discipline as swapvm.md:301-324, 330-346. See
opcodes/extruction.md "Strategy" for the (A)-vs-(B) decision.

For ANY program that begins with Extruction (opcode 0x04, argsLen 0x14, 20-byte target
TGT in [0, 2^160)) followed by an arbitrary symbolic TAIL, execution ends reverted with
reason "ExtructionUnmodelled". TAIL is never decoded: #revert discards the continuation
(swapvm.md:154-156), so its contents cannot affect the conclusion and the proof must
not case-split on it.

PROOF SHAPE — same as gate-spec.k, stop-spec.k, and revert-spec.k. Those three also
quantify over an arbitrary symbolic TAIL because their instruction HALTS (the gate
reverts; Stop sets a sentinel pc; Revert clears the continuation). Extruction shares
that shape: #revert clears the continuation, so an arbitrary tail cannot affect the
conclusion and including one is honest, not a fiction.

The `lengthBytes(TAIL) >=Int 0` side condition is NOT decorative — do not delete. Once
`lengthBytes(b"\x04\x14" +Bytes Int2Bytes(20, TGT, BE) +Bytes TAIL)` rewrites (via the
+Bytes length lemma in lemmas.k) to `22 +Int lengthBytes(TAIL)`, no axiom forces
`lengthBytes` non-negative, so without it the prover can take the termination branch at
<pc> 0 and the claim gets stuck. Same reason as gate-spec.k:27-32, revert-spec.k:18-22,
and stop-spec.k:16-19.

The 2^160 bound on TGT mirrors gate-spec.k:25 — Int2Bytes(20, TGT, BE) is exactly
20 bytes precisely when 0 <= TGT < 2^160, which the round-trip lemma in lemmas.k
relies on. Without the bound the args length is not provably 20 and the canonical-guard
arm of the Extruction rule does not reduce.

Sensitivity twin: extruction-control.k — same premises, conclusion Running instead of
Reverted — must FAIL. Together they show kprove is discriminating on the conclusion.

gate-spec.doc:
Phase 1 go/no-go.

For ANY program that begins with OnlyTakerTokenBalanceNonZero(G) -- with TAIL an
arbitrary, symbolic byte string -- a taker holding zero balance of G ends reverted.

TAIL is never decoded: #revert discards the continuation, so its contents cannot affect
the conclusion and the proof must not case-split on it.

gte-concrete.doc:
Concrete-input conformance claims for the 0x24 (Gte) opcode.

This file replaces the former `gte-spec.k` (a symbolic universal claim) and `gte-control.k`
(its sensitivity twin). Both were TAUTOLOGICAL under the prior predicate-form rule: the spec
assumed `#balanceLtMin(TOK, MIN)` as a premise and the rule branched on the same predicate, so
the proof established nothing about whether the underlying `<` / `>=` definition matched
Solidity, and krun could not reduce the predicate either — i.e. zero conformance evidence.
See gte.md "Direct form, concrete conformance" for the full rationale of the switch.

The direct two-arm rule in `opcodes/gte.k` branches on the REAL comparison
#balanceOf(B, TOK, TAKER) <Int MIN     (REVERT)
#balanceOf(B, TOK, TAKER) >=Int MIN    (PASS)
mirroring the gate's `>Int 0` / `<=Int 0` shape (swapvm.md:182-193) but compared to MIN. A
symbolic universal claim over arbitrary TOK/MIN/TAKER does NOT prove in this form (the K
Haskell backend does not propagate an inequality premise on an uninterpreted-vs-symbolic
comparison into a refutation of the opposite arm — opcodes/deadline.md:125-156). CONCRETE
claims, however, are unaffected: with balance and MIN both concrete Ints, the SMT solver
decides `<Int` / `>=Int` directly and arm selection is immediate. So the two scenarios here
ARE the conformance evidence — they verify the actual comparison against Solidity for fixed
inputs, which the predicate-form symbolic proof could never do.

Each claim runs a FULLY CONCRETE program through `#run` and asserts the exact final `<pc>` and
`<status>`. A concrete claim that proves under kprove is the operational equivalent of having
`krun` the program: it establishes "this exact input reaches this exact state" under the K
rules. The hand-derived expectations here are cross-checked against the Solidity side in
`test/conformance/InstructionConformance.t.sol` (`test_conformance_gte_*`), which runs the
SAME bytes through the REAL `_onlyTakerTokenBalanceGte` body and REAL `runLoop`. Agreement
between the two sides IS the conformance evidence — neither side alone suffices.

PROGRAM CONSTRUCTION. Program = b"\x24\x34" +Bytes Int2Bytes(20, 1, BE) +Bytes
Int2Bytes(32, MIN, BE) (54 bytes total). `b"\x24\x34"` is the [opcode:1][argsLen:1] header —
opcode 0x24 = 36 decimal, argsLen 0x34 = 52 decimal (20-byte token + 32-byte minAmount).
After the decode loop fires <pc> = 2 + 52 = 54. NOTE on the opcode byte: it is `\x24`
(= 36 decimal), NOT `\x36` — the rule keys on the DECIMAL opcode `#exec ( 36 , ARGS )` and
the program byte is the hex literal 0x24 = 36 decimal (0x24 is the unusual case where the hex
and decimal readings diverge by 12, easy to mistype). Arg payloads are built via
`Int2Bytes(N, V, BE)` so the byte widths are exact by construction — hand-typing multi-byte
literals miscounted on the first attempt for other opcodes (see conformance-concrete.k
header). Token value 1 is a PLACEHOLDER: the Solidity side patches the deployed
`GateTokenMock` address into the program at runtime, so `bytes20(1)` here only verifies the
byte plumbing end-to-end. Taker 4660 = address(0x...1234) on the Solidity side.

invalidatetokenout-concrete.doc:
Concrete-input conformance claims for the 0x42 (InvalidateTokenOut) opcode.

Source: `Invalidators.sol:_invalidateTokenOut1D` (lines 122-135). Unlike every modelled
opcode so far this one is NOT a pure conditional halt: it reads the swap registers
(`<amountOut>`, `<balanceOut>`), mutates the `<invalidators>` cell, and — when amountOut
is not yet computed — RECURSES INTO runLoop. The three claims below pin those behaviours
for fully concrete inputs; a claim that proves under kprove is the operational equivalent
of having `krun` the program (see gte-concrete.k / txorigin-concrete.k for the pattern).

PROGRAM. `b"\x42\x00"` — opcode 0x42 = 66 decimal, argsLen 0. Args are IGNORED by the
handler (`bytes calldata /* args */`), so argsLen 0 is the canonical minimal form; the
opcode places no constraint on args length (like 0x53 LimitSwap, unlike the gates). After
decode `<pc>` = 2 + 0 = 2 = program length, so the trailing `#run` halts on the next step.

THE THREE ARMS exercised:
A. Overfill REVERT — amountOut already set, prefilled + amountOut > balanceOut. Immediate
path (`#exec => #checkTokenOut`), arm 2 of #checkTokenOut. (Invalidators.sol:131)
B. PASS + WRITE — the fill fits, the invalidator is updated. Immediate path, arm 3.
Asserts the EXACT final `<invalidators>` map entry. (Invalidators.sol:133)
C. Expects-computed REVERT — amountOut == 0 and the deferred tail computes nothing.
Deferral path (`#exec => #run ~> #checkTokenOut`): the inner #run consumes the (empty)
tail and halts, then arm 1 fires. This is the claim that exercises the RECURSION.
(Invalidators.sol:124-128)

MISSING QUERY FIELDS. The handler reads `ctx.query.maker` / `ctx.query.orderHash`, which
are not `<query>` cells in the K config. They are uninterpreted nullary functions
(`#maker()` / `#orderHash()`, opcodes/invalidatetokenout.k). All three claims pin them
concretely (`requires #maker() ==Int 7` / `#orderHash() ==Int 99`): this is required for
`#prefilledOut` to reduce, because a symbolic key (`invalOut(#maker(), ...)`) into a
concrete map cannot be resolved by the simplifier — the SAME reason txorigin-concrete.k
pins `#txOrigin()`. Pinning makes the lookup key concrete so the [function, total] defining
rule (or its [owise] twin) fires.

jump-control.doc:
DELIBERATELY FALSE. Must fail.

Same program as jump-spec.k -- a 4-byte Jump to TGT in [4, 65535] -- but the conclusion
pins <pc> to 4 (the post-decode value, `2 + argsLen`) instead of TGT (the value the Jump
rule overwrites). This asserts that the Jump rule did NOT fire / did not overwrite <pc> --
i.e. that Jump behaves like Salt or Revert, inheriting the decode-advanced pc.

The Jump rule (opcodes/jump.k) DOES overwrite <pc> (mirroring `pcs = ctx.vm.nextPC` in
VM.sol; swapvm.md:138-140). So this claim is false on every model satisfying the rule: in
the resulting configuration <pc> equals TGT (any value in [4, 65535]) and never equals 4
(since TGT = 4 would require the loop to decode the Jump instruction's own bytes, which is
outside this claim's premise `4 <Int TGT`).

WHY THIS SHAPE. Mirrors negative-control.k, stop-control.k, revert-control.k, and
salt-control.k: the program prefix is concrete (so the prover can actually decode opcode
0x03), the rule fires for real, and the failure is on the conclusion -- not on a stuck
decode. If this control ever PROVES, the rule set is inconsistent (e.g. the Jump rule lost
its `<pc> _ => ...` overwrite) and jump-spec.k above is void (proofs/README.md:20-28).

The sensitivity twin is jump-spec.k itself: same premises, correct conclusion, must prove.
Together they show kprove is discriminating on the conclusion rather than choking on the
setup.

ENV CAVEAT. Like salt-control.k, this control's non-zero exit is the meaningful signal only
when kprove is healthy on the sibling positive claim. In this sandbox kprove has been
observed to die with "Haskell Backend execution failed" when TMPDIR is not /tmp; the task

does. Under that fix the control's failure here is a real counterexample, not incidental.

jump-spec.doc:
Jump overwrites the decode-advanced <pc>.

For a program consisting ONLY of a Jump (opcode 0x03, argsLen 0x02, 2-byte target TGT in
[0, 65535]), execution ends in Running with <pc> == TGT -- NOT 4, the post-decode value
(2 + argsLen). This is the decisive test: the Jump rule (opcodes/jump.k) must OVERWRITE
the <pc> that the decode loop already advanced by `2 + argsLen`, mirroring
`pcs = ctx.vm.nextPC` after dispatch in VM.sol. swapvm.md:138-140 states this directly.

PROOF SHAPE -- WHY THE PROGRAM IS EXACTLY 4 BYTES, WITH NO TAIL.

gate-spec.k, stop-spec.k, and revert-spec.k all quantify over an ARBITRARY symbolic TAIL
because their instruction HALTS (revert clears the continuation; Stop sets a sentinel pc).
Jump does not halt -- it leaves #run in <k>, so the loop proceeds to decode the byte at the
jumped-to <pc>. With an arbitrary tail whose first byte is symbolic, no decode rule reduces
and the prover gets stuck on a residual indistinguishable from a false claim's -- the same
failure mode that sank the first negative-control.k (proofs/README.md:27-34).

The honest shape is to constrain the program so that the JUMP ITSELF lands past the end,
which makes the loop-exit rule (swapvm.md:100-105) fire on the next step without decoding
any further instruction. The minimal such program is exactly the 4-byte Jump:
`b"\x03\x02" +Bytes Int2Bytes(2, TGT, BE)` has length 4, and after the jump <pc> = TGT.
The premise `TGT >=Int 4` (implicit because TGT lands inside [0, 65535] and we need
TGT >= lengthBytes(PGM) = 4 to trigger the loop-exit) makes the loop-exit rule fire on
the next step: <k> becomes .K, <status> stays Running. So the proof closes cleanly.

TGT < 4 would land the jump inside the Jump instruction's own header -- a real corner case
(the real VM would then re-decode the bytes at that position, possibly infinitely). The
claim deliberately scopes to TGT in [4, 65535], so the jump lands past the end and the
program terminates. The behaviour for TGT in [0, 3] is real but out of scope for this
theorem and is left to the conformance harness.

The `lengthBytes(TAIL) >=Int 0` analogue is the bound `0 <=Int TGT` -- load-bearing: without
it the prover cannot establish the loop-exit side condition `TGT >=Int lengthBytes(PGM)`
because lengthBytes(PGM) rewrites to 4 and the SMT solver needs the upper and lower bound
on TGT to discharge `TGT >=Int 4`.

jumpifdirection-control.doc:
DELIBERATELY FALSE. Must fail.

Same program and premises as jumpifdirection-spec.k -- a 5-byte JumpIfDirection with
ARGS[0] = 0x01 and target TGT in (5, 65535], with TIN <Int TOUT so the branch is taken --
but the conclusion pins <pc> to 5 (the post-decode value, `2 + argsLen`) instead of TGT.
This asserts that the jump arm of opcodes/jumps.k did NOT overwrite <pc>, i.e. that
JumpIfDirection behaves like Salt on its taken branch.

The jump arm of opcodes/jumps.k DOES overwrite <pc> when its condition holds (mirroring
`pcs = ctx.vm.nextPC` in VM.sol; swapvm.md:138-140). So this claim is false on every model
satisfying the rule: in the resulting configuration <pc> equals TGT (any value in
(5, 65535]) and never equals 5 (since TGT = 5 is excluded by the strict `5 <Int TGT`
premise, mirroring jump-control.k's `4 <Int TGT`).

WHY THIS SHAPE. Mirrors jump-control.k, negative-control.k, stop-control.k, revert-control.k,
salt-control.k: the program prefix is concrete (so the prover can actually decode opcode
0x30), the rule fires for real, and the failure is on the conclusion -- not on a stuck
decode. If this control ever PROVES, the rule set is inconsistent (e.g. the JumpIfDirection
jump arm lost its `<pc> _ => ...` overwrite) and jumpifdirection-spec.k above is void
(proofs/README.md:20-28).

The sensitivity twin is jumpifdirection-spec.k itself: same premises, correct conclusion,
must prove. Together they show kprove is discriminating on the conclusion rather than
choking on the setup.

jumpifdirection-spec.doc:
0x30 JumpIfDirection overwrites the decode-advanced <pc> when its condition holds.

For a program consisting ONLY of a JumpIfDirection (opcode 0x30, argsLen 0x03, 1-byte
direction = 0x01, 2-byte target TGT in [0, 65535]), when the swapDirection condition holds
-- i.e. when (ARGS[0] =/=Int 0) == (TIN <Int TOUT), which with ARGS[0] = 0x01 reduces to
TIN <Int TOUT -- execution ends in Running with <pc> == TGT, NOT 5 (the post-decode value,
2 + argsLen). This is the conditional twin of proofs/jump-spec.k: the jump arm of
opcodes/jumps.k must OVERWRITE the <pc> that the decode loop already advanced by `2 +
argsLen`, exactly as opcodes/jump.k does for the unconditional Jump.

PROOF SHAPE — why the program is exactly 5 bytes, with no tail. Same logic as jump-spec.k:
JumpIfDirection does not halt — on the taken branch it leaves #run in <k>, so the loop
proceeds to decode the byte at the jumped-to <pc>. With an arbitrary tail whose first byte
is symbolic, no decode rule reduces and the prover gets stuck. The honest shape is to
constrain TGT so the jump lands at or past the end of the program (length 5), which makes
the loop-exit rule (swapvm.md:100-105) fire on the next step. The minimal such program is
`b"\x30\x03" +Bytes b"\x01" +Bytes Int2Bytes(2, TGT, BE)` (length 5), and after the jump
<pc> = TGT >= 5 = lengthBytes(PGM), so the loop-exit rule fires.

TGT in [5, 65535] is the scope (mirrors jump-spec.k's [4, 65535]). TGT < 5 would land the
jump inside the instruction's own bytes -- a real corner case, out of scope here.

The premise `TIN <Int TOUT` makes the jump arm fire: with ARGS[0] = 0x01, the condition
`(ARGS[0] =/=Int 0) ==Bool (TIN <Int TOUT)` reduces to `true ==Bool (TIN <Int TOUT)`, which
holds iff TIN <Int TOUT.

jumpiftokenin-spec.doc:
0x31 JumpIfTokenIn overwrites the decode-advanced <pc> when its condition holds.

For a program consisting ONLY of a JumpIfTokenIn (opcode 0x31, argsLen 0x16, 20-byte token
TOK, 2-byte target TGT in [0, 65535]), when the token-equality condition holds -- i.e.
when Bytes2Int(ARGS[0:20], BE, Unsigned) == tokenIn, which with ARGS = Int2Bytes(20, TOK, BE)
+Bytes Int2Bytes(2, TGT, BE) reduces (via the Bytes2Int/Int2Bytes round-trip lemma in
lemmas.k) to TOK == tokenIn -- execution ends in Running with <pc> == TGT, NOT 24 (the
post-decode value, 2 + argsLen). This is the conditional twin of proofs/jump-spec.k.

PROOF SHAPE — why the program is exactly 24 bytes, with no tail. Same logic as jump-spec.k
and jumpifdirection-spec.k: JumpIfTokenIn does not halt on its taken branch, so the loop

step. The minimal such program is
`b"\x31\x16" +Bytes Int2Bytes(20, TOK, BE) +Bytes Int2Bytes(2, TGT, BE)` (length 24).

The `<tokenIn> TOK </tokenIn>` cell pin plus the premise `0 <=Int TOK andBool TOK <Int
(2 ^Int 160)` makes the jump arm fire: the arm's side condition is
`TIN ==Int Bytes2Int(substrBytes(ARGS, 0, 20), BE, Unsigned)`, which the round-trip lemma
reduces to `TIN ==Int TOK` — satisfied by the cell pin — exactly when TOK is in the 160-bit
unsigned range.

TGT in [24, 65535] is the scope (mirrors jump-spec.k's [4, 65535] and
jumpifdirection-spec.k's [5, 65535]).

jumpiftokenout-spec.doc:
0x32 JumpIfTokenOut overwrites the decode-advanced <pc> when its condition holds.

Structurally identical to jumpiftokenin-spec.k, reading <tokenOut> instead of <tokenIn>.

For a program consisting ONLY of a JumpIfTokenOut (opcode 0x32, argsLen 0x16, 20-byte token
TOK, 2-byte target TGT in [0, 65535]), when Bytes2Int(ARGS[0:20], BE, Unsigned) == tokenOut

Running with <pc> == TGT, NOT 24 (the post-decode value, 2 + argsLen). Conditional twin of

jumpifdirection-spec.k, jumpiftokenin-spec.k: the instruction does not halt on its taken

negative-control.doc:
DELIBERATELY FALSE. Must fail.

Identical to gate-spec.k except the taker's balance is NON-ZERO, so the gate passes and
execution completes Running instead of reverting.

WHY THIS SHAPE. The first version of this control dropped the gate prefix and asserted
that an ARBITRARY program reverts. It did fail -- but for the wrong reason, and it was
therefore worthless. It died at <pc> 0 before a single instruction executed, on a
residual branch where no decode rule applies to a fully symbolic first byte. A review
established the decisive fact: a claim that is TRUE (mere termination over an arbitrary
program) fails with a byte-identical residual. So the old control would have kept
"failing correctly" even if every instruction rule were deleted or made contradictory.

The lesson generalises: a negative control with a SYMBOLIC PREFIX cannot discriminate,
because the prover cannot decode the first instruction. The prefix must be concrete.

This version reaches #exec, consults #balanceOf, and fails with a real computed
counterexample -- <pc> 22, <status> Running.

pricing-negative-control.doc:
DELIBERATELY FALSE. Must fail.

The maker-safety bound with the inequality REVERSED: asserts the taker receives strictly
MORE than the exact rate. Floor division cannot do that. Reaches the arithmetic, unlike
the Phase 1 control that died before any instruction executed.

Runs the whole 3-instruction program, not just the arithmetic: the claim is about what
the VM does, not about what limitQuoteOut computes in isolation.

Both bounds are required. The upper alone is satisfied by returning 0; the lower alone by
returning something huge. Together they pin amountOut to floor(AIN * BOUT / BIN).

privateorder-control.doc:
DELIBERATELY FALSE. Must fail.

Same program and same shape as privateorder-spec.k — opcode 0x2b argsLen 10, packed
taker PACKED in [0, 2^80), arbitrary symbolic TAIL — but the premise fixes the
taker's low 80 bits to EQUAL PACKED (`(TAKER modInt 2^80) ==Int PACKED`), which
selects the PASS arm of the 0x2b rule (opcodes/privateorder.k). The PASS arm leaves
#run in <k> and the loop proceeds to decode the symbolic TAIL; the conclusion
asserts the WRONG post-state (`Reverted("WhitelistInvalidTaker")`). The premise
selects the PASS arm, which does not halt and does not revert, so this claim is
false on every model satisfying the rule: in the resulting configuration <status>
stays `Running` and execution continues into TAIL, never reaching the claimed
Reverted state.

WHY THIS SHAPE. Mirrors negative-control.k (the 0x23 twin), txorigin-control.k
(the 0x26 twin), deadline-control.k, gte-control.k, and supplyshare-control.k: the
program prefix is concrete (so the prover can actually decode opcode 0x2b), the
rule fires for real, and the failure is on the conclusion — not on a stuck decode.
If this control ever PROVES, the rule set is inconsistent (e.g. the 0x2b PASS arm
lost its `==Int` guard, or both arms produce the same outcome) and
privateorder-spec.k above is void (proofs/README.md:20-28).

The sensitivity twin is privateorder-spec.k itself: same program, the OPPOSITE
premise (`=/=Int`), correct conclusion, must prove. Together they show kprove is
discriminating on the arm selected by the premise rather than choking on the setup.

NOTE on the conclusion. Per the convention established in negative-control.k and
followed by txorigin-control.k, this control asserts the SAME Reverted conclusion
as the positive claim (not `Running`), so that its failure is unambiguously
attributable to the arm selected by the premise rather than to a different
post-state assertion. The diagnostic is: the positive claim's premise (`=/=Int`)
selects REVERT and the claim proves; this control's premise (`==Int`) selects PASS,
the rule does not revert, and the Reverted conclusion is never reached.

FIDELITY NOTE. The premise ranges over the taker's low 80 bits (`TAKER modInt 2^80`),
matching the rule's projection. TAKER itself is the full 160-bit address in the
<taker> cell; only its low 80 bits are consulted, faithfully mirroring
`uint80(uint160(taker))`. See opcodes/privateorder.md "The 80-bit packing".

privateorder-spec.doc:
0x2b PrivateOrder — Whitelist.sol:103-110. Positive claim, REVERT direction.

For ANY program that begins with PrivateOrder(PACKED) — with TAIL an arbitrary,
symbolic byte string — a taker whose low 80 bits do NOT equal PACKED ends reverted
with "WhitelistInvalidTaker".

This is the 0x2b twin of gate-spec.k (the 0x23 claim): same shape, same premise
family, the structural difference is that the gate's predicate is an EXTERNAL read
(`#balanceOf(BALS, G, TAKER) ==Int 0`) compared to zero, while this opcode's
predicate is a PURE equality between two decoded values
(`(TAKER modInt 2^80) =/=Int PACKED`). Both select the REVERT arm directly because
the comparison is decidable — `0x23` compares to a constant 0, `0x2b` compares two
terms for equality. The 0x2b rule (opcodes/privateorder.k) is the equality twin of
the 0x23 rule (swapvm.md:182-193).

TAIL is never decoded: #revert discards the continuation (swapvm.md:154-156), so its
contents cannot affect the conclusion and the proof must not case-split on it. Same
shape as gate-spec.k, txorigin-spec.k, deadline-spec.k, and stop-spec.k.

b"\x2b\x0a" is the [opcode:1][argsLen:1] header — opcode 0x2b = 43 decimal, argsLen
0x0a = 10 decimal (the 10-byte packed uint80 allowedTaker). After the decode loop
fires <pc> = 2 + 10 = 12. The packed value itself is constructed via
`Int2Bytes(10, PACKED, BE)` so the round-trip lemma in lemmas.k:64-67 rewrites
`Bytes2Int(Int2Bytes(10, PACKED, BE), BE, Unsigned) => PACKED` exactly, under the
premise `0 <=Int PACKED andBool PACKED <Int 2^80` (which is the lemma's required
bound `0 <=Int V andBool V <Int 2 ^Int (8 *Int N)` with N = 10).

ARM SELECTION — why the premise is `(TAKER modInt 2^80) =/=Int PACKED` and not a
Bool predicate. The 0x2b rule (opcodes/privateorder.k) splits on
(TAKER modInt (2 ^Int 80)) ==Int  Bytes2Int(ARGS, BE, Unsigned)   (PASS)
(TAKER modInt (2 ^Int 80)) =/=Int Bytes2Int(ARGS, BE, Unsigned)   (REVERT)
After the round-trip lemma rewrites `Bytes2Int(Int2Bytes(10, PACKED, BE), ...) =>
PACKED`, both side conditions mention the same two terms
(`TAKER modInt (2 ^Int 80)` and `PACKED`) and split on equality. Equality between
two terms is decidable in the K Haskell backend (SMT-discharged), so the premise
`(TAKER modInt 2^80) =/=Int PACKED` refutes the PASS arm and selects the REVERT arm
directly — exactly as `#balanceOf(...) ==Int 0` selects the 0x23 REVERT arm. The
Deadline/Gte/SupplyShare arm-selection limitation (which forces those opcodes into a
Bool-predicate form) ONLY affects inequalities against SYMBOLIC values; it does not
apply to ==/=/=.

The `lengthBytes(TAIL) >=Int 0` side condition is NOT decorative — do not delete.
Once `lengthBytes(b"\x2b\x0a" +Bytes Int2Bytes(10, PACKED, BE) +Bytes TAIL)`
rewrites to `12 +Int lengthBytes(TAIL)`, no axiom forces `lengthBytes`
non-negative, so without this premise the prover can take the `PC >= length`
termination branch at <pc> 0 and the claim gets stuck. Same reason as
gate-spec.k:27-32, txorigin-spec.k:40-45, deadline-spec.k:37-41, revert-spec.k,
and stop-spec.k.

Sensitivity twin: privateorder-control.k — same program and SAME Reverted
conclusion, premise `(TAKER modInt 2^80) ==Int PACKED` (PASS arm selected) — must
FAIL. Together they show kprove is discriminating on the arm selected by the
premise rather than choking on the setup.

FIDELITY NOTE. The premise ranges over the taker's FULL value TAKER (a 160-bit
address in the <taker> cell) but only its low 80 bits are compared — `modInt 2^80`
discards the high 80 bits, faithfully mirroring `uint80(uint160(taker))`
(Whitelist.sol:106, 83-84). Two takers sharing their low 10 bytes are
indistinguishable to this opcode and to this proof. See opcodes/privateorder.md
"The 80-bit packing" and Whitelist.sol:88-95 for the collision-resistance trade-off.

revert-control.doc:
DELIBERATELY FALSE. Must fail.

Identical program to revert-spec.k -- Revert with a symbolic tail -- but the conclusion
is Running instead of Reverted("InstructionRevert"). Revert is unconditional
(Controls.sol:84-87); it always reverts. So this claim cannot close, and kprove must
report not-proved with a counterexample ending in <status>
Reverted("InstructionRevert") at <pc> 2.

WHY THIS SHAPE. Mirrors negative-control.k and stop-control.k: the program prefix is
concrete (so the prover can actually decode opcode 0x01), the rule fires for real, and
the failure is on the conclusion -- not on a stuck decode. If this control ever PROVES,
the rule set is inconsistent and revert-spec.k above is void (proofs/README.md:20-28).

The sensitivity twin is revert-spec.k itself: same premises, correct conclusion, must
prove. Together they show kprove is discriminating on the conclusion rather than choking
on the setup.

revert-spec.doc:
Revert halts before any tail executes.

For ANY program that begins with Revert (opcode 0x01, argsLen 0x00) followed by an
arbitrary symbolic TAIL, execution ends in Reverted("InstructionRevert"). TAIL is never
decoded: the Revert rule (opcodes/revert.k) produces #revert("InstructionRevert"), and
#revert(MSG) ~> _ => .K (swapvm.md:154-156) clears the continuation so the loop never
resumes.

Shape mirrors gate-spec.k and stop-spec.k: an early-halting instruction makes the tail
irrelevant. The outcome is Reverted, like the gate; the difference is that Revert is
unconditional -- there is no balance side condition, so no extra premise beyond the
generic lengthBytes(TAIL) >=Int 0.

The `lengthBytes(TAIL) >=Int 0` side condition is NOT decorative -- do not delete. Once
`lengthBytes(b"\x01\x00" +Bytes TAIL)` rewrites to `2 +Int lengthBytes(TAIL)`, no axiom
forces `lengthBytes` non-negative, so without it the prover can take the termination
branch at <pc> 0 and the claim gets stuck. Same reason as gate-spec.k:27-32 and
stop-spec.k:16-19.

Sensitivity twin: revert-control.k -- same premises, conclusion Running instead of
Reverted -- must FAIL. Together they show kprove is discriminating on the conclusion.

salt-control.doc:
DELIBERATELY FALSE. Must fail.

Identical program to salt-spec.k's primary claim — Salt with a symbolic 5-byte SALT — but
the conclusion is Reverted("SaltNeverReverts") instead of Running. Salt is a pure no-op
(Controls.sol:72-73); it never reverts. So this claim cannot close, and kprove must report
not-proved with a counterexample ending in <status> Running at <pc> 7.

WHY THIS SHAPE. Mirrors negative-control.k, stop-control.k, and revert-control.k: the
program prefix is concrete (so the prover can actually decode opcode 0x02), the rule fires
for real, and the failure is on the conclusion — not on a stuck decode. If this control
ever PROVES, the rule set is inconsistent and salt-spec.k above is void
(proofs/README.md:20-28).

The sensitivity twin is salt-spec.k itself: same premises, correct conclusion, must prove.
Together they show kprove is discriminating on the conclusion rather than choking on the
setup.

ENV CAVEAT. In this sandbox kprove is broken on every spec (it dies with "Haskell Backend
execution failed with code 1" even on the untouched gate-spec.k), so the control's non-zero
exit here is the same broken-kprove failure mode, not on its own meaningful discrimination.
The meaningful signal is the hand-trace: Salt produces Running and never Reverted, so the
control's conclusion is false by direct evaluation of the rule. See the task brief's
"Critical environment facts" #2.

salt-spec.doc:
T4 — Salt is a pure no-op; its args contribute nothing at execution time.

For ANY 5-byte SALT (symbolic, constrained only by lengthBytes(SALT) ==Int 5) following the
Salt header (opcode 0x02, argsLen 0x05), execution ends in Running with <pc> advanced to
7 — the post-decode position 2 + argsLen. The SALT bytes are passed to #exec as ARGS but
the Salt rule (opcodes/salt.k) matches them with a wildcard and never inspects them, so
their concrete values cannot affect the conclusion. This is the salt-args analogue of the
gate theorem's "the tail is irrelevant".

DEVIATION FROM THE GATE-SPEC SHAPE — semantic, not stylistic. gate-spec.k, stop-spec.k,
and revert-spec.k all quantify over an ARBITRARY symbolic TAIL because their instruction
HALTS (the gate reverts and clears the continuation; Stop sets a sentinel pc; Revert clears
the continuation). Salt does NONE of these — it leaves #run in <k>, so the loop proceeds to
decode the byte at pc 7. With a symbolic TAIL that byte is symbolic and no decode rule
reduces, so the prover gets stuck at the next step with a byte-identical residual (the same
failure mode that sank the first negative-control.k — proofs/README.md:27-34). An arbitrary
tail therefore CANNOT be part of a clean terminating claim for Salt; including one would be
stating a fiction, which this repo does not do. See opcodes/salt.md "Composition".

The claim terminates because lengthBytes(b"\x02\x05" +Bytes SALT) rewrites (via the
+Bytes length lemma in lemmas.k) to 2 +Int lengthBytes(SALT) = 7, so at pc 7 the loop-exit
rule (swapvm.md:100-105) fires and <k> becomes .K.

lengthBytes(SALT) ==Int 5 is load-bearing: without it the program length is symbolic and
the loop-exit check `7 >=Int lengthBytes(PGM)` cannot reduce. It plays the same role for
this claim that `lengthBytes(TAIL) >=Int 0` plays for gate-spec.k — the side condition that
lets the length reasoning close.

stop-control.doc:
DELIBERATELY FALSE. Must fail.

Identical program to stop-spec.k -- Stop with a symbolic tail -- but the conclusion is
Reverted("...") instead of Running. Stop is the unconditional-SUCCESS halt
(Controls.sol:89-93); it never reverts. So this claim cannot close, and kprove must
report not-proved with a counterexample ending in <status> Running at <pc> 2.

WHY THIS SHAPE. Mirrors negative-control.k: the program prefix is concrete (so the
prover can actually decode opcode 0x00), the rule fires for real, and the failure is on
the conclusion -- not on a stuck decode. If this control ever PROVES, the rule set is
inconsistent and stop-spec.k above is void (proofs/README.md:20-28).

The sensitivity twin is stop-spec.k itself: same premises, correct conclusion, must
prove. Together they show kprove is discriminating on the conclusion rather than
choking on the setup.

stop-spec.doc:
T3 -- Stop halts before any tail executes.

For ANY program that begins with Stop (opcode 0x00, argsLen 0x00) followed by an
arbitrary symbolic TAIL, execution ends in Running with <k> cleared. TAIL is never
decoded: the Stop rule clears the continuation (mirroring #revert at swapvm.md:154-156),
so the loop never resumes and the tail cannot affect the conclusion.

<pc> ends at the post-decode value (2), exactly like the Revert twin
(proofs/revert-spec.k:28). The Solidity sets nextPC = type(uint256).max, but that value is
an implementation detail of the loop-exit mechanism; what a proof can observe is that the
loop halted with Running status. See opcodes/stop.k for why modelling the literal max
stalls the prover on giant-constant arithmetic.

Shape mirrors gate-spec.k: an early-halting instruction makes the tail irrelevant. The
outcome is Running, not Reverted, because Stop is the unconditional-success halt.

The `lengthBytes(TAIL) >=Int 0` side condition is NOT decorative -- do not delete. Once
`lengthBytes(b"\x00\x00" +Bytes TAIL)` rewrites to `2 +Int lengthBytes(TAIL)`, no axiom
forces `lengthBytes` non-negative, so without it the prover can take the termination
branch at <pc> 0 and the claim gets stuck. Same reason as gate-spec.k:27-32.

supplyshare-concrete.doc:
Concrete-input conformance claims for the 0x25 (SupplyShare) opcode.

This file replaces the former `supplyshare-spec.k` (a symbolic universal claim) and
`supplyshare-control.k` (its sensitivity twin). Both were TAUTOLOGICAL under the prior
predicate-form rule: the spec assumed `notBool #supplyShareSufficient(...)` as a premise
and the rule branched on the same predicate, so the proof established nothing about
whether the underlying conjunction `totalSupply > 0 && balance * 1e18 >= minShare *
totalSupply` matched Solidity, and krun could not reduce the predicate either — i.e.
zero conformance evidence. See supplyshare.md "Direct form, concrete conformance" for
the full rationale of the switch. Same trade the Gte subagent made for the same reasons
(proofs/gte-concrete.k header, opcodes/gte.md "Direct form, concrete conformance").

The direct two-arm rule in `opcodes/supplyshare.k` branches on the REAL conjunction
totalSupply >Int 0  AND  balance *Int 1e18 >=Int minShare *Int totalSupply   (PASS)
NOT( ... )                                                                 (REVERT)
A symbolic universal claim over arbitrary TOK/MIN/TAKER does NOT prove in this form
(the K Haskell backend does not propagate an inequality premise on an
uninterpreted-vs-symbolic comparison into a refutation of the opposite arm —
opcodes/deadline.md:125-156, opcodes/gte.md "Arm selection"). CONCRETE claims,
however, are unaffected: with `#balanceOf`, `#totalSupply`, and MIN all reduced to
concrete Ints — the first via the defining rule on a concrete `<balances>` cell, the
second via a spec premise, the third via a concrete `Int2Bytes(8, MIN, BE)` payload —
the whole conjunction becomes a concrete arithmetic fact the SMT solver decides
immediately, exactly as for the Gte concrete claims (proofs/gte-concrete.k). The 1e18
multiplications are concrete; SMT handles them directly. So the two scenarios here ARE
the conformance evidence — they verify the actual arithmetic against Solidity for fixed
inputs, which the predicate-form symbolic proof could never do.

Each claim runs a FULLY CONCRETE program through `#run` and asserts the exact final
`<pc>` and `<status>`. A concrete claim that proves under kprove is the operational
equivalent of having `krun` the program: it establishes "this exact input reaches this
exact state" under the K rules. The hand-derived expectations here are cross-checked
against the Solidity side in `test/conformance/InstructionConformance.t.sol`
(`test_conformance_supplyShare_*`), which runs the SAME bytes through the REAL
`_onlyTakerTokenSupplyShareGte` body and REAL `runLoop`. Agreement between the two
sides IS the conformance evidence — neither side alone suffices.

PROGRAM CONSTRUCTION. Program = b"\x25\x1c" +Bytes Int2Bytes(20, 1, BE) +Bytes
Int2Bytes(8, MIN, BE) (30 bytes total). `b"\x25\x1c"` is the [opcode:1][argsLen:1]
header — opcode 0x25 = 37 decimal, argsLen 0x1c = 28 decimal (20-byte token + 8-byte
minShareE18). After the decode loop fires <pc> = 2 + 28 = 30. Arg payloads are built
via `Int2Bytes(N, V, BE)` so the byte widths are exact by construction — hand-typing
multi-byte literals miscounted on the first attempt for other opcodes (see
conformance-concrete.k header). Token value 1 is a PLACEHOLDER: the Solidity side
patches the deployed mock token address into the program at runtime, so `bytes20(1)`
here only verifies the byte plumbing end-to-end. Taker 4660 = address(0x...1234) on the
Solidity side, matching the Gte concrete claims so the same mock fixture shape applies.

MOCK TOKEN GAP (Solidity side — NOT this file's scope, flagged for the integrator per
the brief). `Controls.sol:174-175` consults BOTH `IERC20(token).balanceOf(taker)` AND
`IERC20(token).totalSupply()`. The current Solidity conformance fixture
`GateTokenMock` (test/conformance/InstructionConformance.t.sol:16-22) exposes ONLY
`balanceOf`; it has no `totalSupply`. To run the Solidity mirror of these two K claims
the integrator must extend `GateTokenMock` to expose `totalSupply` (e.g. add a
`uint256 public totalSupply;` field with a `setTotalSupply(uint256)` setter that also
implements the ERC-20 `totalSupply()` selector, or rename the mock and inherit a
minimal ERC-20). `bytes20(1)` is a placeholder the integrator patches to the deployed
mock's address at runtime, exactly as for the Gte claims. `bytes8(1e18)` is
`bytes8(uint64(1e18))` — Solidity-side uint64 cast mirrors the K-side `Int2Bytes(8,
MIN, BE)` round-trip with the lemma's `0 <=Int MIN <Int 2^64` bound.

txorigin-concrete.doc:
Concrete-input conformance claims for the 0x26 (TxOrigin) opcode.

This file is the concrete twin of `txorigin-spec.k` (the symbolic go/no-go claim that
holds for any TAIL). It runs TWO fully-concrete fixed-byte programs through `#run`,
pins `#txOrigin()` to a concrete value via a premise, and asserts the exact final
`<pc>` and `<status>`. A concrete claim that proves under kprove is the operational
equivalent of having `krun` the program: it establishes "this exact input reaches this
exact state" under the K rules. The hand-derived expectations here are cross-checked
against the Solidity side in `test/conformance/InstructionConformance.t.sol`
(`test_conformance_txOrigin_*`), which runs the SAME bytes through the REAL
`_onlyTxOriginTokenBalanceNonZero` body and REAL `runLoop`. Agreement between the two
sides IS the conformance evidence — neither side alone suffices.

This is the tx.origin twin of the 0x23 concrete-claim family: same program shape
(opcode 0x26 + argsLen 0x14 + 20-byte token), same two scenarios (REVERT on zero
balance, PASS on positive balance), same pc post-decode value (2 + 20 = 22). The ONLY
structural difference is that the balance consulted is
`#balanceOf(BALS, TOK, #txOrigin())` (uninterpreted environment EOA,
opcodes/txorigin.k) rather than `#balanceOf(BALS, TOK, TAKER)` (the <taker> cell).

ARM SELECTION — why `requires #txOrigin() ==Int 771` is enough. The 0x26 rule
(opcodes/txorigin.k) splits on
#balanceOf(B, TOKEN, #txOrigin()) >Int 0     (PASS)
#balanceOf(B, TOKEN, #txOrigin()) <=Int 0    (REVERT)
i.e. it compares the balance to a CONSTANT (0). The `#txOrigin()` symbol is the only
uninterpreted piece inside `#balanceOf`, and fixing it via a concrete premise makes the
whole `#balanceOf` application reduce to a concrete int via the defining rule
(swapvm.md:171-174): {B [ bal(TOKEN, 771) ] orDefault 0}:>Int. Once that is concrete,
the `>Int 0` / `<=Int 0` split decides immediately, exactly as it does for the 0x23
concrete claims where TAKER is concretised by the <taker> cell read. The tx.origin
VALUE itself (771) is environment, supplied on the Solidity side by `vm.txOrigin =
0x...0303`; this K premise is the matching abstraction-boundary pin. See
`conformance-concrete.k` for the established pattern.

PROGRAM CONSTRUCTION. Program = b"\x26\x14" +Bytes Int2Bytes(20, 1, BE) (22 bytes
total). The arg payload is built via `Int2Bytes(N, V, BE)` so the byte width is exact
by construction — hand-typing multi-byte literals miscounted on the first attempt for
other opcodes (see conformance-concrete.k header). Token value 1 is a PLACEHOLDER: the
Solidity side patches the deployed `GateTokenMock` address into the program at runtime,
so `bytes20(1)` here only verifies the byte plumbing end-to-end. Scenario A uses
`<balances> .Map </balances>` — the `#balanceOf` `[owise]` rule (swapvm.md:174) returns
0 for the missing `bal(1, 771)` key, selecting the REVERT arm. Scenario B uses
`<balances> bal(1, 771) |-> 5 </balances>` so `#balanceOf = 5 >Int 0`, selecting the
PASS arm.

conclusion is never reached.

ENV CAVEAT. Like deadline-control.k and the other sibling controls, this control's
non-zero exit is the meaningful signal only when kprove is healthy on the sibling
positive claim. In this sandbox kprove has been observed to die with "Haskell Backend
execution failed" when TMPDIR is not /tmp; the brief's "Critical environment facts"
directs setting TMPDIR=/tmp, which the run harness does. Under that fix the control's
failure here is a real counterexample, not incidental.

txorigin-spec.doc:
Phase 1 sibling of gate-spec.k. For ANY program that begins with
OnlyTxOriginTokenBalanceNonZero(G) — with TAIL an arbitrary, symbolic byte string — a
tx.origin holding zero balance of G ends reverted with "TxOriginTokenBalanceIsZero".

This is the tx.origin twin of gate-spec.k (the 0x23 claim): same shape, same
premise family, the only structural difference is that the balance consulted is
`#balanceOf(BALS, G, #txOrigin())` (uninterpreted environment EOA, opcodes/txorigin.k)
rather than `#balanceOf(BALS, G, TAKER)` (the <taker> cell). The opcode 0x26 rule
(opcodes/txorigin.k) is byte-for-byte identical to the 0x23 rule (swapvm.md:182-193)
modulo that one argument.

TAIL is never decoded: #revert discards the continuation (swapvm.md:154-156), so its
contents cannot affect the conclusion and the proof must not case-split on it. Same
shape as gate-spec.k, deadline-spec.k, and stop-spec.k.

b"\x26\x14" is the [opcode:1][argsLen:1] header — opcode 0x26 = 38 decimal, argsLen
0x14 = 20 decimal (the uint160 token). After the decode loop fires <pc> = 2 + 20 = 22.
The token value itself is constructed via `Int2Bytes(20, TOK, BE)` so the round-trip
lemma in lemmas.k:64-67 rewrites `Bytes2Int(Int2Bytes(20, TOK, BE), BE, Unsigned) =>
TOK` exactly, under the premise `0 <=Int TOK andBool TOK <Int 2^160` (which is the
lemma's required bound `0 <=Int V andBool V <Int 2 ^Int (8 *Int N)` with N = 20).

ARM SELECTION — why the premise is `#balanceOf(BALS, TOK, #txOrigin()) ==Int 0` and
not a Bool predicate. The 0x26 rule (opcodes/txorigin.k) splits on
#balanceOf(B, TOKEN, #txOrigin()) >Int 0     (PASS)
#balanceOf(B, TOKEN, #txOrigin()) <=Int 0    (REVERT)
i.e. it compares an uninterpreted function application to a CONSTANT (0). This is the
same form as the 0x23 gate (swapvm.md:182-193), which proves in the direct two-arm
form because constant reasoning IS propagated into arm refutation. The
Deadline/Gte/SupplyShare arm-selection limitation (which forces those opcodes into a
Bool-predicate form) ONLY affects inequalities against SYMBOLIC values; it does not
apply here. So a premise `#balanceOf(BALS, TOK, #txOrigin()) ==Int 0` selects the
REVERT arm directly — exactly as `#balanceOf(BALS, G, TAKER) ==Int 0` selects the
gate's REVERT arm in gate-spec.k.

The `lengthBytes(TAIL) >=Int 0` side condition is NOT decorative — do not delete.
Once `lengthBytes(b"\x26\x14" +Bytes Int2Bytes(20, TOK, BE) +Bytes TAIL)` rewrites to
`22 +Int lengthBytes(TAIL)`, no axiom forces `lengthBytes` non-negative, so without
this premise the prover can take the `PC >= length` termination branch at <pc> 0 and
the claim gets stuck. Same reason as gate-spec.k:27-32, deadline-spec.k:37-41,
revert-spec.k, and stop-spec.k.

Sensitivity twin: txorigin-control.k — same program and premises, conclusion
`Running` instead of `Reverted("TxOriginTokenBalanceIsZero")` — must FAIL. Together
they show kprove is discriminating on the conclusion rather than choking on the
setup.

whitelistcoequal-concrete.doc:
Concrete-input conformance claims for the 0x2c (WhitelistCoequal) opcode.

This file replaces the former `whitelistcoequal-spec.k` (a symbolic universal claim) and
`whitelistcoequal-control.k` (its sensitivity twin). Both were TAUTOLOGICAL under the prior
uninterpreted-predicate form: the spec asserted `#coequalWhitelistContains(ARGS, PACKED)` as
a premise and the rule branched on the same predicate, so the proof established nothing
about whether the underlying `while (i-- > 0)` loop matched Solidity, and krun could not
reduce the predicate either — i.e. zero conformance evidence. See whitelists.md "What the
K rules do" for the full rationale of the switch.

The recursive `#coequalContains(LIST, PACKED)` function in `opcodes/whitelists.k` now models
the Solidity loop directly:
sender = uint80(uint160(taker)) = TAKER modInt 2^80
list   = ARGS[2:]                                  // post-header slice
for each 10-byte entry e in list (high-index first):
if (sender == e) JUMP;
FALL THROUGH.
On CONCRETE lists the recursion reduces to a concrete Bool via the bytes lemmas in
semantics/lemmas.k (lines 16-67: `lengthBytes`, `substrBytes`, and the `Int2Bytes`/
`Bytes2Int` round-trip), so the rule arm fires for the right reason. On SYMBOLIC lists
neither rule's `requires` clause reduces, so the function is STUCK — no false symbolic
claim is admitted. This is the same posture as gte-concrete.k: concrete claims are the
conformance evidence; symbolic claims are honestly stuck rather than wrong.

Each claim runs a FULLY CONCRETE program through `#run` and asserts the exact final `<pc>`
and `<status>`. A concrete claim that proves under kprove is the operational equivalent of
having `krun` the program: it establishes "this exact input reaches this exact state" under
the K rules. The hand-derived expectations here are cross-checked against the Solidity side
in `test/conformance/InstructionConformance.t.sol` (`test_conformance_whitelist_coequal_*`),
which runs the SAME bytes through the REAL `_whitelistCoequal` body and REAL `runLoop`.
Agreement between the two sides IS the conformance evidence — neither side alone suffices.

PROGRAM CONSTRUCTION. Program = b"\x2c\x0c" +Bytes Int2Bytes(2, 14, BE) +Bytes
Int2Bytes(10, ENTRY, BE) (14 bytes total). `b"\x2c\x0c"` is the [opcode:1][argsLen:1] header
— opcode 0x2c = 44 decimal, argsLen 0x0c = 12 decimal (2-byte pc + 10-byte packed entry,
N=1). The pc field is `Int2Bytes(2, 14, BE)` = uint16 BE of 14, so `args.parseWhitelistCoequalPC()`
returns 14 — exactly the program length, so the JUMP lands past the end and the loop-exit
rule (swapvm.md:100-105) fires on the next step. The packed entry is `Int2Bytes(10, ENTRY, BE)`
so the function's `Bytes2Int(substrBytes(LIST, 0, 10), BE, Unsigned)` reduces to ENTRY via
the round-trip lemma (lemmas.k:65) under the bound `0 <=Int ENTRY andBool ENTRY <Int 2^80`,
which holds for both ENTRY=4660 (scenario A) and ENTRY=9999 (scenario B).

taker 4660 = address(0x...1234). The packed taker is `4660 modInt 2^80 = 4660` (4660 < 2^80),
matching the rule's `TAKER modInt (2 ^Int 80)` projection faithfully. Scenario A pins the
entry to the taker's packed bits (JUMP); scenario B pins it elsewhere (FALL THROUGH). Both
end at <pc> 14 = program length: scenario A because the jump target IS 14 (past end → loop
exit), scenario B because the FALL-THROUGH arm inherits the decode-advanced pc
(2 + argsLen = 2 + 12 = 14, also past end → loop exit).

whitelistsequential-concrete.doc:
Concrete-input conformance claims for the 0x2d (WhitelistSequential) opcode.

This file replaces the former `whitelistsequential-spec.k` (a symbolic universal claim) and
`whitelistsequential-control.k` (its sensitivity twin). Both were TAUTOLOGICAL under the
prior uninterpreted-predicate form: the spec asserted `#sequentialWhitelistJumps(ARGS, PACKED)`
as a premise and the rule branched on the same predicate, so the proof established nothing
about whether the underlying time-aware `while (i < length)` loop matched Solidity, AND
krun could not reduce the predicate either — i.e. zero conformance evidence. See
whitelists.md "What the K rules do" for the full rationale of the switch.

The recursive `#seqOutcome(LIST, TIMELEFT, PACKED)` function in `opcodes/whitelists.k` now
models the Solidity loop directly:
sender = uint80(uint160(taker)) = TAKER modInt 2^80
start  = Bytes2Int(ARGS[2:7], BE, Unsigned)              // 5-byte start timestamp
list   = ARGS[7:]                                          // post-header slice
timeLeft = block.timestamp - start                        // preconditions: ts >= start
for each 12-byte entry (duration, allowedTaker) in list (low-index first):
if (sender == allowedTaker) JUMP;                     // addr at LIST[2:12]
if (timeLeft < duration)   REVERT;                    // dur at LIST[0:2]
timeLeft -= duration;
FALL THROUGH.
On CONCRETE lists + a CONCRETE timestamp the recursion reduces to a concrete outcome tag
(#WL_JUMP / #WL_REVERT / #WL_FALLTHROUGH) via the bytes lemmas in semantics/lemmas.k
(lines 16-67: `lengthBytes`, `substrBytes`, and the `Int2Bytes`/`Bytes2Int` round-trip), so
the rule arm fires for the right reason. On SYMBOLIC lists neither rule's `requires` clause
reduces, so the function is STUCK — no false symbolic claim is admitted. This is the same
posture as gte-concrete.k and whitelistcoequal-concrete.k: concrete claims are the
conformance evidence; symbolic claims are honestly stuck rather than wrong.

Each claim runs a FULLY CONCRETE program through `#run` and asserts the exact final `<pc>`
and `<status>`. A concrete claim that proves under kprove is the operational equivalent of
having `krun` the program: it establishes "this exact input reaches this exact state" under
the K rules. The hand-derived expectations here are cross-checked against the Solidity side
in `test/conformance/InstructionConformance.t.sol`
(`test_conformance_whitelist_sequential_*`), which runs the SAME bytes through the REAL
`_whitelistSequential` body and REAL `runLoop`. Agreement between the two sides IS the
conformance evidence — neither side alone suffices.

PROGRAM CONSTRUCTION. Program = b"\x2d\x13" +Bytes Int2Bytes(2, 21, BE) +Bytes
Int2Bytes(5, 0, BE) +Bytes Int2Bytes(2, 1000, BE) +Bytes Int2Bytes(10, ENTRY, BE)
(21 bytes total). `b"\x2d\x13"` is the [opcode:1][argsLen:1] header — opcode 0x2d = 45
decimal, argsLen 0x13 = 19 decimal (2-byte pc + 5-byte start + (2-byte dur + 10-byte entry)
for N=1). The pc field is `Int2Bytes(2, 21, BE)` = uint16 BE of 21, so the JUMP arm lands
at pc=21, which is EXACTLY the program length (21 bytes), so the loop-exit rule
(swapvm.md:100-105) fires on the next step. The start field is `Int2Bytes(5, 0, BE)` =
40-bit BE of 0, so `ts >=Int 0` for any non-negative timestamp premise. The duration field
is `Int2Bytes(2, 1000, BE)` = uint16 BE of 1000. The packed entry is
`Int2Bytes(10, ENTRY, BE)` so the function's `Bytes2Int(substrBytes(LIST, 2, 12), BE,
Unsigned)` reduces to ENTRY via the round-trip lemma (lemmas.k:65) under the bound
`0 <=Int ENTRY andBool ENTRY <Int 2^80`, which holds for both ENTRY=4660 (scenario A) and
ENTRY=9999 (scenario B).

TIMESTAMP PREMISE. `#blockTimestamp()` is `[function, no-evaluators]` (opcodes/whitelists.k)
— its value is fixed-but-unknown, so each claim pins it via the premise
`requires #blockTimestamp() ==Int 10`. This is what makes the `#seqOutcome` recursion
reduce: with timestamp=10 and start=0, `timeLeft = 10 - 0 = 10`, a concrete Int; the
`timeLeft <Int duration` check then reduces to `10 <Int 1000` → true. On the Solidity side
this premise corresponds to `vm.warp(10)` in the conformance test
(InstructionConformance.t.sol), which sets `block.timestamp` to 10.

taker 4660 = address(0x...1234). The packed taker is `4660 modInt 2^80 = 4660` (4660 <
2^80), matching the rule's `TAKER modInt (2 ^Int 80)` projection faithfully. Scenario A
pins the entry to the taker's packed bits (JUMP before the duration check fires); scenario
B pins it elsewhere (REVERT via `timeLeft(10) < duration(1000)`). Both end at <pc> 21 =
program length: scenario A because the jump target IS 21 (past end → loop exit), scenario B
because the REVERT arm inherits the decode-advanced pc (2 + argsLen = 2 + 19 = 21, also
past end → the halt rule fires after `<k>` is cleared).

xycswap-concrete.doc:
Concrete-input conformance claims for the 0x50 (XYCSwap) opcode.

Source: `XYCSwap.sol:_xycSwapXD`. The constant-product pricer (x*y=k curve, no fees) — a
direct structural sibling of `0x53` LimitSwap. The four claims below pin all four arms for
fully concrete inputs; a claim that proves under kprove is the operational equivalent of
having `krun` the program (see gte-concrete.k / pricing-spec.k for the pattern). The exact-
out claim deliberately picks a non-dividing input so the CEILING is exercised (43, not 42).

PROGRAM. `b"\x50\x00"` — opcode 0x50 = 80 decimal, argsLen 0. Args are IGNORED by the
handler (`bytes calldata /* args */`), so argsLen 0 is the canonical minimal form; the
opcode places no constraint on args length (like 0x53 LimitSwap, unlike the gates). After
decode `<pc>` = 2 + 0 = 2 = program length, so the trailing `#run` halts on the next step.

THE FOUR ARMS exercised:
A. Exact-in pricing — amountOut = (amountIn * balanceOut) / (balanceIn + amountIn), floored.
100 * 100 / (100 + 100) = 50. (XYCSwap.sol exact-in branch.)
B. Exact-out pricing — amountIn = ceilDiv(amountOut * balanceIn, balanceOut - amountOut).
ceilDiv(30 * 100, 100 - 30) = ceilDiv(3000, 70) = 43 (3000/70 = 42 remainder 60, so
ceiling is 43 — NOT 42, which distinguishes ceiling from floor).
C. Both-balances-zero revert — balanceIn 0, reverts "XYCSwapRequiresBothBalancesNonZero".
D. Recompute revert — exact-in with amountOut already set, reverts "XYCSwapRecomputeDetected".

HAND-COMPUTED QUOTES (cross-checked against the Solidity curve):
A. xycQuoteOut(100, 100, 100) = 10000 / 200 = 50          (exact, floor = 50)
B. xycQuoteIn(30, 100, 100)  = ceilDiv(3000, 70) = 43      (non-dividing: 42 r.60 -> 43)

dustproof-control.doc:
DELIBERATELY FALSE. Must FAIL.

D1 with the maker-safety bound REVERSED: it asserts the taker receives strictly MORE than
the exact curve value. Floor division cannot do that, so this must never prove.

WHY A CONTROL AT ALL. A proof that cannot fail proves nothing, and the worst failure mode
-- an inconsistent rule set -- proves EVERYTHING while looking like total success. This is
the only check that catches it. If this ever returns #Top, D1 is worthless and so is every
other theorem over the same definition.

WHY THIS SHAPE. It keeps the CONCRETE program prefix and every hypothesis of D1, changing
only the conclusion. proofs/README.md records why that matters: the first control written
in this project failed at `<pc> 0`, before a single instruction executed, on a residual
branch where no decode rule applies to a symbolic first byte -- and a review established
that a claim which is TRUE fails with a byte-identical residual. It would have kept
"failing correctly" with every instruction rule deleted. A control with a symbolic prefix
cannot discriminate; this one reaches the arithmetic and fails on the value.

Its sensitivity twin is D1 itself: same premises, correct conclusion, must PROVE. The pair
is what shows kprove is discriminating on the conclusion rather than choking on the setup.

dustproof-spec.doc:
D1 -- the DustProof order quotes EXACTLY the constant-product floor.

The program is the whole shape `DustOrderBuilder` emits, and nothing else:

0x23 0x14 <20-byte gateToken>   OnlyTakerTokenBalanceNonZero   pc  0 -> 22
0x20 0x05 <5-byte deadline>     Deadline                       pc 22 -> 29
0x50 0x00                       XYCSwap                        pc 29 -> 31
0x02 0x08 <8-byte salt>         Salt                           pc 31 -> 41

This is the theorem the product rests on: for ANY maker reserves and ANY trade size, a
taker who passes the gate and beats the deadline receives exactly
`floor(amountIn * balanceOut / (balanceIn + amountIn))`. Not "at most", not "about" --
exactly, to the wei.

WHY BOTH BOUNDS. The first alone is satisfied by quoting zero; the second alone by
quoting something enormous. Together they pin ?AOUT uniquely as the floor. This is the
same two-sided shape as T1 (pricing-spec.k), and for the same reason: a one-sided bound
is not a specification of a curve, it is a list of things a conservative quote happens
to satisfy.

NO StaticBalances, DELIBERATELY. In Aqua mode the maker's funds stay in their wallet and
Aqua supplies the balances, so `AquaOpcodes` does not dispatch `StaticBalances` at all.
The claim therefore takes `<balanceIn>`/`<balanceOut>` as symbolic and UNCHANGED rather
than as something the program writes -- which is both the faithful model of Aqua mode and
a stronger statement, since it quantifies over every reserve pair Aqua could supply.

THE GATE IS FIRST, and that is load-bearing rather than stylistic. T0 (gate-spec.k) is
stated over programs BEGINNING with `0x23 0x14 G` with an arbitrary symbolic tail, so it
already covers this program: a taker holding zero `G` reverts before any pricing happens.
D1 is the complement -- what happens on the path where the gate PASSES. Move the gate
later in the program and T0 stops applying, which is why the builder fixes the order
instead of taking it as a parameter.

`#blockTimestamp() <=Int DL` is the not-expired branch. The expired branch reverts
`DeadlineReached` and is covered separately; stating both in one claim would collapse
them into a disjunction that proves less about either.
